subject: physics

turns.reply: Welcome, I'm glad you're here! Think about a street lamp that switches itself on as it gets dark: what do you think makes it turn on?

turns.student: omg my phone battery's dead i swear
turns.reply: Ha, a dead phone is a good reminder that batteries push electric charge round circuits. Look at the diagram: a resistor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin, meaning double the push gives double the flow. If the push were tripled, what would happen to the flow?
turns.diagramCaption: A resistor at constant temperature: a straight line through the origin.

turns.reply: The origin is the point on a graph where both quantities are zero, usually the bottom-left corner. So a line through the origin means no push gives no flow. If the push is zero on this graph, how much flow would there be?

turns.student: zero i guess? like if nothings pushing it nothings gonna move
turns.reply: Yes, zero is right: with no push, nothing moves, which is why the line passes through the origin. If the push on an ohmic conductor is doubled, what happens to the flow?

An ohmic conductor is a component whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature. Because of that, its graph is a straight line through the origin, so double the push gives double the flow. If the push on an ohmic conductor is tripled, what happens to the flow?
That's fair, it's a lot of new stuff. Do you want to stop here, do one more quick thing, or switch to the slides?
Thanks for sticking with it. For an ohmic conductor, double the push gives double the flow. Say your dead phone's charger gives the push. If the push is tripled, what happens to the flow?

turns.student: it like... triples too? cause double makes it double so triple makes it triple
turns.reply: Yes, the flow triples too. You spotted the pattern from "double gives double," and that's exactly how an ohmic conductor works. Well done, and you can come back to this any time. That was the quick one. Do you want to stop here, or keep going?

Let's go. A variable resistor lets you change the resistance by hand, by sliding a contact along a track. That's how a volume control or dimmer switch works. If you slide it so the resistance goes up, what happens to the current?

Current is how much electric charge flows round the circuit each second. Think of cars passing under a bridge: more cars each second means a bigger current. It's the "flow" you tripled earlier. Back to the volume control on your phone. If the resistance goes up, what happens to the flow?
This bit is a tricky one, so no worries. Do you want me to just tell you the rest of this one?
Think of your phone's volume slider. Sliding it changes the resistance, and that changes how much current flows. When you slide the volume down, what happens to the resistance?

turns.student: lol my volume's always at max anyway
turns.reply: Max is fine, the slider still shows the idea. If you slide a dimmer to make a lamp dimmer, what has happened to the current?
